1.goal: To open on something she already has an opinion about, and to say once where the hour ends.
1.interaction: T–S, open question. Whole class of one, no writing.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class and whether anything in it was unclear.
Say, once, what today is: she reads two reviews of the same film and then recommends something of her own, out loud, with two reasons.
Ask the question on screen. Take the title and one sentence about it, no more.
exact: About the pre-class: “Did you open the pre-class? Was anything hard?”
What today is: “Today you read two reviews. Then you recommend something you watched — with two reasons.”
If she names something and stops: “Would you tell a friend to watch it?”
1.expected: A title, and a yes or no. She will probably not add a reason yet, and that is the point of the hour.
1.support: If nothing comes to mind, offer two: the last thing she finished, or the last thing she gave up on.
1.challenge: Ask who she would recommend it to, and who she would not.
1.monitoring: Whether a reason appears without being asked for. This is the baseline of the whole block.
1.evidence: Whether a reason came unprompted, and how many sentences she produced in one turn.
1.transition: Move on as soon as she has named something and heard what today is.

2.goal: To make the difference between an answer that ends the conversation and one that keeps it going audible before any reading happens.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the five lines on screen together.
run: Read the brief with her.
Read the five answers out loud, one by one, and ask which ones actually answer the question.
Do not correct one by one — close it at the end with the two that carry a reason.
exact: Closing the two: “These two do the same thing: they say what you think and then why. That is the whole lesson.”
2.expected: The second and the fourth. “It is good”, “Yeah” and “I do not know” end the conversation.
2.support: If she picks the short ones, ask what the other person could possibly say next after “Yeah”.
2.challenge: Ask which of the two she is more likely to say herself, and why.
2.monitoring: Whether she can hear the difference before she can produce it.
2.evidence: Whether she recognizes the reason as the part that does the work.
2.transition: Move on once the two useful answers are named.

3.goal: To have her risk a guess about why two people disagree, before she reads a word of them.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. No right answers yet.
run: Read the three questions on screen with her.
Take one guess on each. Do not confirm and do not correct — these are hypotheses.
Write her two guesses down somewhere she can see them; the reading confirms or refutes them.
exact: If she risks nothing: “Guess: is it about the story, or about the people?”
Before moving on: “That is your guess. Now we read and see if you were right.”
3.expected: Rough guesses about acting, story, length, ending. Whether both can be right is the interesting one.
3.support: If she risks nothing, offer two and let her choose. Choosing is still risking.
3.challenge: Ask whether a bad review can be useful to someone who ends up liking the film.
3.monitoring: Whether she guesses without being sure. She tolerates error well, so this should be easy for her.
3.evidence: Her two predictions, kept for the next screen.
3.transition: Move on when all three have an answer, right or wrong.

4.goal: To read both reviews once for the general position, without stopping on any word.
run: Give her a minute and a half for both. Say out loud that she should not stop on any word.
Ask which one recommends the film and which one does not.
Ask which of her guesses from the screen before turned out to be right.
exact: Before she reads: “Read both once. Do not stop on any word — you only need to know who says yes.”
4.expected: Maya recommends it, Chris does not. That is all this screen asks for.
4.support: If she stalls on a word, tell her to skip it and keep going, and come back to it at the end if it still matters.
4.challenge: Ask which review she would have written, before she looks at the reasons.
4.monitoring: Whether she reads for the whole before the parts, or tries to decode line by line. Nothing in the previous seventeen lessons asked her to read on her own, so this is the first thing you will know about it.
4.evidence: How long she takes, and whether she stops on individual words.
4.transition: Move on once she has named who says yes.

5.goal: To attribute each reason to its author, going back to the text to prove it.
5.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S to check.
run: Let her do the six on her own before you say anything.
Check them one by one. On each, ask her to point at the line in the review that proves it.
Spend the time on the last one — the photography. It is the one that teaches something.
exact: On the photography item: “Chris did not like the film. So why is this sentence in his review?”
5.expected: Five come out easily. The photography line goes to Chris, and that usually surprises.
5.support: If she is stuck, narrow it: “Who talks about time — the one who liked it or the one who did not?”
5.challenge: Ask her to find the one thing both reviews mention. It is the ending.
5.monitoring: Whether she goes back to the text to sustain an answer, or answers from memory.
5.evidence: Whether she returns to the text when asked to prove something.
5.transition: Move on when the six are placed and the photography one has been discussed.

6.goal: To separate what the reviews say from what she assumes they say.
6.interaction: S alone, then T–S to check.
run: Let her mark the three on her own.
Check them. On each true one, ask for the line.
The cinema item is the one that is nowhere in the text — make that explicit when you get to it.
6.expected: True: both talk about the ending, Chris finds something good, Chris finds the story predictable. The other three are not in the text or say the opposite.
6.support: If she marks the cinema one, ask her to find the word “cinema” in either review.
6.challenge: Ask what else the two reviews would have to say for them to be about different films.
6.monitoring: Whether she distinguishes what is written from what sounds likely. This comes back in the fourth block.
6.evidence: Which of the three false ones she marked, if any.
6.transition: Move on once the three are settled.

7.goal: To notice that the lines of a review do three different jobs, before anyone names them.
run: Let her sort the six lines on her own.
Check them, and ask what makes a reason a reason: what can the other person do with it?
Do not name the rule yet — the next screen does that.
7.expected: Two opinions, two reasons, two recommendations. The long Chris line is the one most often called an opinion.
7.support: Ask, on each line: could someone argue with this? Opinions cannot be argued with; reasons can be used.
7.challenge: Ask which of the three jobs is missing from most of what people say when asked about a film.
7.monitoring: Whether she can see the function of a line and not just its content.
7.evidence: Whether she identifies the reason as the usable part without being told.
7.transition: Move on when the six are sorted and she has said, in her own words, what a reason does.

8.goal: To make the point of the whole lesson visible: the opinion alone convinces nobody.
run: Read the two opinions on screen, alone, with the reasons covered.
Ask the question: with only these two lines, would she watch the film?
Open the reveal and read the two full sentences. The difference should be obvious by now.
8.expected: She cannot decide from the opinions alone. That is the answer the screen is looking for.
8.support: If she says she would decide anyway, ask her what she would be deciding on.
8.challenge: Ask which of the two full sentences she finds more convincing, and why.
8.monitoring: Whether the point lands as something she noticed rather than something she was told.
8.evidence: Her own formulation of why the reason matters. Write it down in her words if it is good.
8.transition: Move on to production as soon as the reveal has been read.

9.goal: To produce one whole sentence — opinion plus reason — about four things she chooses.
9.interaction: T–S, oral, one prompt at a time.
run: Name one of the four things on screen. She answers in one sentence.
Take all four, one after the other, without stopping to correct.
Praise the whole sentence, not the correct word. The sentence is what the block is measuring.
exact: If she answers with an opinion only: “Good. Now say it again with the reason in the same sentence.”
9.expected: Four sentences with a reason in each. The frames are on screen and she may use them.
9.support: If she stops after the opinion, give the first two words of the reason and let her finish.
9.challenge: Ask for one of the four without any of the frames on screen.
9.monitoring: Whether the reason comes in the same breath or as a second turn after a prompt.
9.evidence: How many of the four carried a reason unprompted.
9.transition: Move on when all four have been said.

10.goal: To add a second, different reason without waiting to be asked.
run: Ask her to take one of the four things she just talked about and say it again with a second reason.
Use the box on screen to check the second reason is really a second one, and not the first one repeated.
Do it twice, with two different things.
exact: If the second reason repeats the first: “That is the same reason in other words. Give me a different one — about the ending, or the people, or the length.”
10.expected: Two sentences in one turn, with two different reasons. This is the hardest thing on the screen and the point of the lesson.
10.support: Offer three categories to pick a second reason from: the people, the story, or how long it is.
10.challenge: Ask for a third reason, or for a reason she thinks someone else would give.
10.monitoring: Whether she can tell two reasons apart from one reason said twice.
10.evidence: Whether a second, distinct reason appeared, and whether it needed prompting.
10.transition: Move on when she has produced two distinct reasons at least once.

11.goal: To recommend something she chose, to a person who has never heard of it, with two reasons and nothing on the screen.
11.interaction: T–S, sustained. She talks, you listen and do not correct.
run: Give her one minute to decide what she will talk about and, if she wants, to write two words down. She likes preparation time; one minute is enough here.
Ask her to tell you about it as if you had never heard of it. Do not interrupt for language.
When she finishes, ask two questions about the thing itself — not about English.
Only then, if she stalled, point her to the reveal button with the sentence starters.
exact: Opening the task: “I have never heard of this. Tell me what it is, what you think, and why — and tell me what I should do about it.”
If she stops after two sentences: “And what else? Give me the other reason.”
11.expected: Three to five sentences at least: what it is, what she thinks, two reasons, a recommendation. Two or three sentences is where she has been until now, so anything past that is the result.
11.support: The starters are behind a button, closed. Open them only if she stalls, let her look, and close them again — with them on screen she reads instead of speaking.
11.challenge: Ask her to convince you when you say you do not usually like that kind of thing.
11.monitoring: Count the sentences. Count the reasons. Note whether she asked how to say a word, and which word.
11.evidence: How many sentences in one turn, how many distinct reasons, and whether the screen stayed closed. This is the main record of the lesson.
11.transition: Move on when she has finished and answered your two questions.

12.goal: To give one point of feedback and run the task again under a harder condition.
run: Write down one thing that worked and one thing to build on. One, not three.
Put her first version and a clearer version of the same sentence side by side in the boxes.
Open the replay. This time you have already seen it and you did not like it — she keeps her two reasons and admits one thing you are right about.
exact: Opening the replay: “I watched it. I did not like it. Convince me anyway.”
12.expected: The same two reasons, plus one concession. The concession is new and will need the line on screen the first time.
12.support: Point at the line on screen and let her use it as it is on the first attempt.
12.challenge: Do not accept the first concession if it is not really a concession — ask what she actually agrees with.
12.monitoring: Whether the reasons survive the pressure of disagreement, or shrink to one.
12.evidence: Whether she conceded a point and still held her position. It is the first sign of the third block.
12.transition: Move on when the second version has been said.

13.goal: To close the lesson with what was worked on and where it goes.
13.interaction: T–S, ticking the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself — it is hers, not yours.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud: decide what she would say about the next thing she finishes, before she closes it.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “Next time you finish an episode, before you close it, decide what you would say about it — and the reason.”
13.expected: Her own reading of what she can and cannot do yet. It may be lower than what you saw.
13.support: If she marks everything low, name one specific thing she did today that she could not do an hour ago.
13.challenge: Ask which of today's phrases she would actually use in Portuguese too.
13.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed. The gap is worth noting.
13.evidence: Her confidence marks, and anything she said about the pre-class.
13.transition: End here. The next lesson opens with the same two people, talking.
